studies.evidence_quote: “Participants were randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to an alternate-day fasting group, daily calorie restriction group, or no-intervention control group.” The Results report: “Of the 222 participants who were screened, 100 (45.0%) were randomly assigned to the diet or control groups,” with 34 assigned to alternate-day fasting, 35 to daily calorie restriction, and 31 to control. “The primary outcome of the study was change in body weight.”
studies.page_or_section: Methods: Randomization and Intervention Groups; Methods: Outcome Measures; Results
studies.treatment_group_label: Alternate-day fasting (n=34) and daily calorie restriction (n=35)
studies.results_location: Results sections: Participant Characteristics and Attrition; Prescribed vs Actual Energy Intake (Figure 2); Percentage Energy Restriction; Physical Activity and Dietary Intake; Weight Loss and Weight Maintenance (Figure 3 and Table 2); Blood Pressure and Heart Rate; Plasma Lipids; Glucoregulatory and Inflammatory Factors
studies.description: A single-center, three-arm randomized clinical trial tested whether one year of alternate-day fasting produced better adherence, weight loss/maintenance, and cardiovascular risk profiles than daily calorie restriction or no intervention. The same cohort underwent a 6-month weight-loss phase followed by a 6-month weight-maintenance phase; these phases were not independent studies.

primary_outcomes: Expression of 82 preselected genes in subcutaneous adipose tissue at baseline and week 12
studies.evidence_quote: Overall, 150 overweight or obese nonsmokers (50% women) were recruited for the study comprising a 12-wk intervention phase, a 12-wk maintenance phase, and a 26-wk follow-up phase. Participants were assigned to 1 of the 3 study arms (ICR, CCR, or Control) in a ratio of 1:1:1 by stratified block randomization... As the primary endpoint, we defined differences in the expression of 82 preselected genes in subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) between ICR and CCR assessed at baseline and week 12. The 150 participants were randomly assigned to either ICR (n = 49), CCR (n = 49), or Control group (n = 52).
studies.page_or_section: Methods—Study design and participants; Results—Baseline characteristics
studies.treatment_group_label: Intermittent calorie restriction (ICR; n=49) and continuous calorie restriction (CCR; n=49)
studies.control_group_label: Control regimen with no prescribed calorie restriction (n=52)
studies.results_location: Results sections: Baseline characteristics (Table 1, Figure 1); Compliance to calorie restriction (Supplemental Table 6, Supplemental Figure 1); Intervention effects on body weight (Figure 2); Intervention effects on changes in SAT gene expression (Table 2, Supplemental Table 2); Intervention effects on circulating biomarkers (Table 3); Sensitivity analyses; Sustainability of intervention effects across maintenance and follow-up phases (Figures 3–4, Supplemental Table 7, Supplemental Figure 2); HR-QoL and side effects (Supplemental Figure 3, Supplemental Table 8).
studies.description: The single HELENA randomized controlled trial compared a 5:2 intermittent calorie-restriction regimen with continuous daily calorie restriction and a no-restriction control over 50 weeks. It tested whether intermittent restriction produced stronger changes in adipose-tissue gene expression and assessed longer-term anthropometric, body-composition, metabolic, and quality-of-life outcomes.

primary_outcomes: Percentage change in body weight from baseline to month 6
studies.evidence_quote: The trial was a 6-month, single-center, randomized clinical trial... Participants were randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to a TRE, CR, or control group... We conducted an intention-to-treat analysis, which included data from all 75 participants who underwent randomization.
studies.page_or_section: Methods: Trial Participants; Randomization and Blinding; Statistical Analysis
studies.treatment_group_label: 8-hour time-restricted eating (TRE; n=25) and 25% daily calorie restriction (CR; n=25)
studies.results_location: Results sections: Trial Participants; Weight Loss and Body Composition; Glycemic Control and Medication Effect Score; Sensitivity Analysis Using Multiple Imputation; Plasma Lipid Levels and Blood Pressure; Adherence and Energy Intake; Daily Eating Window, Diet Quality, and Physical Activity; Adverse Events. Statistics are also presented in the Study Flowchart, Change in Body Composition and Glycemic Control in the Study Groups figure, Body Weight, Glycemic Control, and Cardiometabolic Risk Factors table, and supplementary eTables 1-3/eFigures 2-3.
studies.description: A single 6-month, three-arm, parallel randomized clinical trial tested whether 8-hour TRE without calorie counting produced greater weight loss and improved glycemic control compared with 25% daily calorie restriction or a usual-habits control in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

primary_outcomes: Absolute change in body weight from baseline to month 12
studies.evidence_quote: “This is a 12-month prospective, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial... Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to a TRE, CR, or control group.” The Participants section reports “90 adults with obesity,” and Outcomes and Follow-up states: “The primary outcome was absolute change in body weight between the TRE, CR, and control groups by month 12.”
studies.page_or_section: Methods: Design Overview; Setting and Participants; Outcomes and Follow-up
studies.treatment_group_label: Time-restricted eating (TRE; n=30) and calorie restriction (CR; n=30)
studies.control_group_label: Control (baseline eating window of ≥10 hours/day; n=30)
studies.results_location: Results: Trial Participants; Weight Loss and Body Composition; Glucoregulatory Factors, Blood Pressure, and Plasma Lipids; Sensitivity Analyses Using Multiple Imputation; Adherence, Energy Intake, and Physical Activity; Adverse Events. Also participant flow diagram, figure “Change in body weight and energy intake between groups over 12 months,” and tables “Change in Body Weight and Body Composition From Baseline and Between Intervention Groups,” “Change in Metabolic Disease Risk Variables From Baseline and Between Intervention Groups,” and “Dietary Intake and Physical Activity Between Groups Over 12 Months.”
studies.description: A single 12-month, three-arm randomized controlled trial tested whether an 8-hour time-restricted eating regimen without calorie counting produced greater weight loss and cardiometabolic improvements than daily 25% calorie restriction or a no-intervention control in racially and ethnically diverse adults with obesity.

studies.evidence_quote: Twenty-four male war veterans were recruited and consented to participate in this pilot trial... The study consisted of a single centre, parallel group randomised controlled trial. Participants were randomised to one of two groups - A standard energy restricted diet (SERD) or an intermittent energy restricted 5:2 diet group (5:2 DIET)... Measurements were taken at baseline and at three and six months.
studies.page_or_section: Methods; Results
studies.treatment_group_label: Intermittent energy restricted 5:2 diet (5:2 DIET)
studies.results_location: Results section; Table 1 (demographics, clinical characteristics, and anthropometric/biochemical outcomes); Table 2 (symptoms); Table 3 (dietary intake); Figure 1 (CONSORT flow); Figure 2 (quality-of-life scores)
studies.description: A single-centre, parallel-group randomized pilot trial tested whether six months of a 5:2 intermittent-energy-restriction diet could produce at least 5% weight loss and greater anthropometric and biochemical improvements than standard daily energy restriction in older obese male war veterans. Twenty-four men were randomized equally between the two diets, and 23 completed the six-month trial.

studies.evidence_quote: Overweight females (n 121) 18 y were randomized 1:1 to either IER [2-d 500 kcal (2100 kJ); n 61] or CER [1500 kcal (6000 kJ); n 60] in this 12-mo noninferiority trial. ... The primary outcome was weight loss and secondary outcomes were BMI, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level, fasting glucose and insulin levels, HOMA-IR score, and 2-h oral-glucose-tolerance test (OGTT) results.
studies.page_or_section: Abstract (Methods); Methods—Clinical measurements; Methods—Statistics
studies.treatment_group_label: Intermittent energy restriction (IER): 500 kcal/day on 2 nonconsecutive days per week
studies.control_group_label: Continuous energy restriction (CER): 1500 kcal/day, 7 days per week
studies.results_location: Results—Weight loss and Secondary outcomes; Table 2 (primary and secondary outcomes); Figure 2 (participant flow); Table 3 (dietary intake and physical activity); Results—Physical activity and sleep quality
studies.description: A single 12-month randomized noninferiority trial tested whether intermittent energy restriction produced weight loss no worse than continuous daily energy restriction in overweight women with a history of gestational diabetes, while also comparing diabetes-risk markers and related behavioral outcomes.

studies.treatment_group_label: Intermittent fasting (2510 kJ/600 kcal on two 24-hour periods per week; eating to appetite on other days)
studies.control_group_label: Continuous moderate energy restriction (30% below estimated weight-maintenance energy needs)
primary_outcomes: Body composition (trunk fat and lean body mass)
studies.evidence_quote: “This was a 52-week stratified, randomised parallel group pilot study... Ten participants with type 1 diabetes and overweight or obesity were recruited to the study; five in each arm.”
studies.page_or_section: Methods (opening paragraph and Sections 2.1–2.4); Results, Sections 3, 3.1, and 3.2
studies.results_location: Results Sections 3.1 (Safety) and 3.2 (Efficacy); Table 2 (changes from baseline at 12 and 52 weeks), with baseline data in Table 1
studies.description: A single randomized parallel-group pilot study compared the safety and efficacy of intermittent fasting with continuous daily energy restriction for weight loss in adults with type 1 diabetes and overweight or obesity. The active weight-loss phase lasted 12 weeks, followed by observation through week 52.

primary_outcomes: Change in intrahepatic triglyceride (IHTG) content from baseline to 6 and 12 months
studies.evidence_quote: A total of 88 eligible patients with obesity and NAFLD ... were randomly assigned to the TRE (n = 45) or DCR (n = 43) group. The primary outcome was change in the IHTG content from baseline to 6 and 12 months.
studies.page_or_section: Methods—Study Design, Outcomes; Results—opening paragraph and Primary Outcome
studies.treatment_group_label: Time-restricted eating (TRE; prescribed calories consumed from 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM)
studies.control_group_label: Daily calorie restriction (DCR; same prescribed caloric intake with habitual meal timing/no eating-time restriction)
secondary_outcomes: Body fat percentage and fat mass
studies.results_location: Results—Primary Outcome, Weight Loss and Body Fat, Metabolic Risk Factors and Liver Enzymes, and Adverse Events; Figure 2; Tables 2 and 3; Supplement 2 eTables 1–3 and eFigures 1–2
studies.description: A single 12-month, parallel-group, observer-blinded randomized clinical trial tested whether 8-hour time-restricted eating provides greater reductions in liver fat and metabolic risk than daily calorie restriction among adults with obesity and NAFLD. The 6- and 12-month assessments are follow-ups of the same randomized sample, not independent studies.

primary_outcomes: Feasibility of the intermittent fasting intervention
Percent body weight lost from baseline to 6-month follow-up (initial effectiveness)
Intervention adherence (sessions attended and self-monitoring booklets completed)
studies.evidence_quote: A total of 42 Black adults with a BMI≥25 were recruited from five Black churches (3 IF churches, 2 CER churches)... The primary outcome was feasibility, consisting of initial effectiveness on body weight (percent body weight lost from baseline to 6-month follow-up), adherence, and acceptability. A cluster randomized controlled design was used... Black churches were randomized to either a 6-month... IF intervention, or a 6-month... CER intervention.
studies.page_or_section: Abstract; Methods—Study Design of the Pilot Study; Results
studies.treatment_group_label: Intermittent Fasting (IF; 5:2 fasting intervention)
secondary_outcomes: Body mass index and body composition (body fat, muscle mass, visceral fat)
Waist and hip circumference and waist-to-hip ratio
Dietary intake (energy, fat, fruit and vegetables, fiber)
Obesity-related plasma biomarkers (glucagon, GLP-1, leptin, adiponectin, adipsin, lipocalin-2/NGAL, resistin, PAI-1, CRP)
studies.results_location: Results—Participant characteristics (Table 1); Changes in body weight and other anthropometric measures and Changes in obesity-related health behaviors (Table 2; Supplementary Figure 3); Changes in obesity-related biomarkers (Tables 2–3; Supplementary Figure 4); Intervention Adherence; Intervention Acceptance; participant flow in Figure 2
studies.description: This single cluster-randomized pilot study randomized five Black churches and 42 participants to a 6-month IF intervention or a CER comparison intervention. It tested whether the culturally and faith-adapted IF program was feasible in Black churches based on preliminary effectiveness, adherence, and acceptability, while also comparing anthropometric, behavioral, and metabolic outcomes.

primary_outcomes: Change in HbA1c from baseline to 6 months
studies.evidence_quote: “A randomised, parallel group controlled clinical trial was conducted...” and “With one participant withdrawing, 51 participants were randomised (26 to TRE and 25 to DIET [Figure S2]).” The prespecified primary outcome was “the change in HbA1c between baseline and six months.”
studies.page_or_section: Sections 2.1 (Study design), 2.8 (Sample size and statistical analysis), and 3 (Results)
studies.treatment_group_label: Time-restricted eating (TRE; eating between 1000 and 1900 h)
studies.control_group_label: Individualised dietetic practice/guidance (DIET; active standard-care comparator)
secondary_outcomes: Fasting glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, and other blood metabolites/hormones
Physical activity and sleep/time in bed
Blood pressure and resting heart rate
studies.results_location: Section 3 (Results), especially Table 1; Figures 2 and 3; Table 2; Supplementary Tables S1–S5 and Figures S2–S7
studies.description: One six-month, two-arm parallel randomised controlled trial compared time-restricted eating with individualised dietetic guidance in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight/obesity. It tested whether TRE was non-inferior to standard dietetic practice for improving HbA1c, while also assessing body composition, glycaemic metrics, dietary behaviour, and adherence.

primary_outcomes: Change in bodyweight at 3 months of intervention
Change in bodyweight after the subsequent 3-month follow-up
studies.evidence_quote: “The trial was a single-centre, parallel, superiority, open-label randomised controlled clinical trial… Individuals were randomly assigned 1:1 to 3 months of 10-h TRE or habitual living… 100 participants… were enrolled and randomly assigned (50 to each group)… The primary outcome of change in bodyweight was assessed after 3 months (12 weeks) of the intervention… and after 3 months (13 weeks) of follow-up.”
studies.page_or_section: Methods—Study design, Randomisation and masking, and Outcomes; Results
studies.treatment_group_label: 10-h per-day time-restricted eating (TRE)
studies.results_location: Results section; Figure 1 (trial profile), Table 2 (timing and adherence), Table 3 and Figure 3 (primary and secondary outcomes); per-protocol and exploratory results in appendix pp 3–4
studies.description: A single parallel-group randomized controlled trial tested whether 3 months of a self-selected 10-hour daily eating window, compared with habitual living, reduced bodyweight and improved cardiometabolic risk factors in adults at high risk of type 2 diabetes. The same randomized cohort was reassessed after a further 3-month intervention-free follow-up; this was not a separate data-collection sample.

studies.treatment_group_label: Daily caloric restriction (DCR; n=15) or intermittent fasting (IMF; n=13)
studies.results_location: Results—Human study (Enrollment and baseline clinical characteristics; Feasibility, safety, acceptability, and tolerability; Circulating and PBMC markers; Magnetic resonance imaging); Tables 1–3 and S1–S5; Figures 1 and 3A/C
studies.description: A one-year randomized pilot feasibility trial in adults with ADPKD and overweight/obesity comparing behavioral weight-loss interventions based on daily caloric restriction versus intermittent fasting. It primarily assessed intervention feasibility, adherence, safety, acceptability/tolerability, and weight loss, with exploratory kidney-volume and adiposity outcomes.
studies.evidence_quote: “Twenty-eight participants were randomized to a behavioral weight loss intervention based on either DCR or IMF.” The paper states: “Our primary goal was to determine the feasibility of a behavioral weight loss intervention based on DCR or IMF in adults with ADPKD and overweight or obesity.”
studies.page_or_section: Results, Human study, pp. 2–5; Discussion, p. 9

studies.treatment_group_label: DCR (n=7), TRF (n=7), or IMF (n=9)
studies.results_location: Results—Animal study (all four subsections); Figures 2, 3B/D, and S2–S4
studies.description: A parallel 3-month feeding trial in Pkd1RC/RC ADPKD mice compared daily caloric restriction, time-restricted feeding, and intermittent fasting with ad libitum feeding. It tested effects on weight, health measures, cystic kidney disease progression, and relevant signaling pathways.
studies.evidence_quote: The study used mice “adhering to either ad libitum feeding (AL), daily caloric restriction (DCR), time restricted feeding (TRF), or intermittent fasting (IMF).” Figure 2 reports: “N: AL (8M, 4F), DCR (3M, 4F), TRF (3M, 4F), IMF (4F, 5M).”
studies.page_or_section: Results, Animal study, pp. 5–9; Figure 2 caption, p. 8

primary_outcomes: Change from baseline to month 6 in postprandial glucose area under the curve (AUC) during a mixed-meal tolerance test
studies.evidence_quote: This open-label, three-arm, parallel group sequential randomized controlled trial was conducted between 26 September 2018 and 30 November 2021 and involved a 6-month intervention phase followed by a 12-month follow-up. The primary objective for this study was to assess differences in glucose tolerance in response to a mixed-meal in iTRE versus CR at 6 months. Eligible participants ... were randomized to either iTRE or CR or standard care (2:2:1 ratio). In total, 209 participants ... were enrolled ...: 85 ... were allocated to iTRE, 83 ... were allocated to CR and 41 ... were allocated to standard care.
studies.page_or_section: Methods—Study design and participants; Results—Trial participants (pp. 963–965 and online Methods)
studies.treatment_group_label: Active dietary interventions: intermittent fasting plus early time-restricted eating (iTRE; n=85) and daily calorie restriction (CR; n=83); the prespecified primary comparison was iTRE versus CR
secondary_outcomes: Total cholesterol, HDL, LDL, and total cholesterol-to-HDL ratio
Physical activity and self-reported dietary intake
studies.results_location: Results sections ‘Glycemic control,’ ‘Cardiovascular risk,’ ‘Liver health,’ ‘Body weight and composition,’ ‘Physical activity and self-reported dietary intake,’ ‘Follow-up data at 18 months,’ and ‘Safety outcomes’; Tables 2–4; Figures 1–2; Extended Data Figures 1–3 and Supplementary Tables 1–7
studies.description: A single three-arm randomized controlled trial tested whether 6 months of iTRE improved mixed-meal postprandial glucose tolerance more than daily calorie restriction in adults at elevated risk of type 2 diabetes, with standard care as an inactive comparator. Participants were additionally followed for 12 months after the supported intervention, making month 18 a follow-up of the same cohort rather than a separate study.

primary_outcomes: Adherence to the 8-hour time-restricted eating window at month 12 (percentage adhering within ±30 minutes)
secondary_outcomes: Body weight and percentage weight loss
Dietary intake and Healthy Eating Index
Safety, adverse events, quality of life, and mood
studies.evidence_quote: “A 1-year, randomized, two-arm, single-blind pilot study was conducted… We hypothesized that 75% of participants in the TRE group would adhere to the 8-hour window (primary outcome).” The Results state: “Of the 29 randomized individuals, 23 completed the study, including 71% (n 10) of those in the TRE group and 87% (n 13) in the HE group.”
studies.page_or_section: Materials and Methods—Experimental design, Participants, and Primary outcome measures; Results—Participants and Adherence and safety
studies.treatment_group_label: Time-restricted eating (TRE; 8-hour eating window beginning within 3 hours of waking)
studies.control_group_label: Healthy eating advice without time restriction (HE)
studies.results_location: Results sections “Participants,” “Adherence and safety,” “Clinical measurements and self-reported questionnaires,” and “Dietary intake and Healthy Eating Index”; Tables 2–6; Figures 1–4; Supplementary Tables 4–5 and Supplementary Figure 1
studies.description: A single 12-month randomized parallel-group pilot trial tested the feasibility and effects of an 8-hour time-restricted eating intervention versus healthy-eating advice without meal-timing restriction in adults with ADPKD. The primary objective was whether at least 75% of TRE participants adhered to the prescribed eating window.

studies.treatment_group_label: Hypoenergetic diet + 12-hour time-restricted feeding (HD+TRF)
studies.evidence_quote: “This study is a randomized, parallel, controlled clinical trial, with two research groups, with a 12 months follow-up period.” The baseline table reports “Characteristics of the participants at the beginning of the intervention (n 58)” with HD n=27 and HD+TRF n=31. The Introduction states: “the primary objective of this study was to evaluate the long-term effects of the TRF regimen on body weight... Body composition and vital signs were also measured as secondary outcomes.”
studies.page_or_section: Sections 1 (Introduction), 2.2 (Study design), 2.5–2.7 (Randomization, Intervention, Outcome), and 3 (Results)
studies.results_location: Section 3 (Results), Tables 2 and 3, and Figure 2; participant allocation and attrition in Figure 1 and baseline data in Table 1
studies.description: A single 12-month randomized parallel-group clinical trial tested whether adding a daily 12-hour time-restricted feeding window to an individualized hypoenergetic diet affected weight loss in low-income women with obesity, compared with the same energy-restricted diet without time restriction. Body composition and vital signs were assessed as secondary outcomes.

studies.treatment_group_label: Zero-calorie alternate-day fasting (ADF)
primary_outcomes: Body composition (fat mass, trunk fat mass, lean mass)
Blood lipids (total cholesterol, HDL, LDL, triglycerides)
studies.evidence_quote: Adults with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m², age 18-55) were randomized to either zero-calorie ADF (n=14) or CR (-400 kcal/day, n=12) for 8 weeks. Outcomes were measured at the end of the 8-week intervention and after 24 weeks of unsupervised follow-up. The primary aim of this pilot study was to evaluate the safety and tolerability of an 8-week zero-calorie ADF intervention.
studies.page_or_section: Abstract; Methods—Experimental Design; Results
studies.results_location: Figure 1; Tables 2–6; Results subsections: Study Enrollment and Attrition, Safety Assessments, Energy and Macronutrient Intake, Body Weight and Body Composition, Resting Metabolic Rate, Lipids and Insulin Sensitivity, and Leptin, Ghrelin, and BDNF
studies.description: One randomized parallel-group pilot study compared eight weeks of zero-calorie alternate-day fasting with moderate daily caloric restriction in adults with obesity. Outcomes were assessed after treatment and again after a 24-week unsupervised follow-up; the follow-up was part of the same cohort, not a separate study.

primary_outcomes: Change in body weight at 12 months
studies.evidence_quote: “In total 112 participants ... were randomized to intermittent or continuous energy restriction.” The Methods further state: “The primary endpoint was change in body weight after one year,” and Table 1 reports 54 participants assigned to intermittent restriction and 58 to continuous restriction.
studies.page_or_section: Methods—Participants, Randomization, Study design, and Outcome measures; Results—Study participants and Study outcomes
studies.treatment_group_label: Intermittent energy restriction (400/600 kcal for women/men on two non-consecutive days per week)
studies.control_group_label: Continuous energy restriction (equivalent weekly energy reduction distributed across seven days)
secondary_outcomes: Change in body weight at 6 months
studies.results_location: Results—Study participants, Study outcomes, Adverse events, Energy intake/physical activity/resting metabolic rate, and Feelings of hunger and well-being; Figure 1; Tables 2–4; Supplementary eTable 1
studies.description: A single 1-year randomized controlled trial compared intermittent 5:2 energy restriction with an equivalent continuous daily energy restriction among adults with abdominal obesity and at least one additional metabolic-syndrome component. It assessed weight loss over six months, maintenance through 12 months, and changes in cardiometabolic risk factors and subjective hunger.

studies.treatment_group_label: Alternate-day modified fasting (ADMF) plus remotely delivered exercise
studies.control_group_label: Continuous energy restriction with a low-calorie diet (LCD) plus remotely delivered exercise
primary_outcomes: Feasibility (participant retention, intervention attendance, and adherence)
Body composition change (fat mass, body fat percentage, fat-free mass, and leg lean mass)
secondary_outcomes: Physical function (timed chair stands, grip strength, balance, Liver Frailty Index, and Karnofsky Performance Status)
Diet difficulty, hunger, quality of life, and participant satisfaction
studies.evidence_quote: “This trial was a 24-week, parallel-arm, randomized controlled trial. Eligible participants were randomized to follow ADMF or a control diet using continuous energy restriction with a LCD.” Results further state: “Sixty individuals were screened and 20 were randomized to either the continuous low-calorie diet (LCD; n = 9) or alternate-day modified fasting (ADMF; n = 11; Figure 1).”
studies.results_location: Results §§3.1–3.5; Figure 1 (participant flow), Figure 2 (attendance/adherence), Table 2 and Figures 3–4 (weight, body composition, cardiometabolic, liver, and functional outcomes)
studies.description: A single 24-week pilot parallel-arm randomized trial compared alternate-day modified fasting with continuous low-calorie restriction in adults with obesity and Child-Pugh Class A non-alcoholic cirrhosis; both arms also received the same remotely delivered exercise and behavioral-support program. The trial primarily evaluated feasibility and safety and also assessed weight loss, body composition, physical function, and liver/cardiometabolic outcomes.

studies.evidence_quote: Participants (n=81...) were randomized to E-TRE (10-hour eating window starting within 3 hours of waking) plus DCR or DCR alone (~35% daily caloric restriction) for 39 weeks. The primary outcome was body weight (measured with digital scale) at week 12.
studies.page_or_section: Abstract; Methods—Study Design and Sample Size Determination and Power Analysis
studies.treatment_group_label: Early time-restricted eating plus daily caloric restriction (E-TRE+DCR)
secondary_outcomes: Body weight and body composition at week 39
Body composition (fat mass and fat-free mass)
Blood lipids (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides)
studies.results_location: Results—Adherence, Meal Timing, Body weight by clinic or home scale, Body weight and composition by DXA, Energy Intake and HEI, Appetite and Eating Behaviors, Activity Behaviors, Resting Energy Expenditure, and Metabolic Outcomes; Tables 2–4 and S1–S6; Figures 2–4 and S1–S5
studies.description: One parallel-group randomized trial tested whether adding a prescribed early 10-hour eating window to an approximately 35% daily caloric-restriction behavioral weight-loss program improved weight loss and related metabolic and behavioral outcomes compared with daily caloric restriction alone over 39 weeks.
